title: A Review of Time Series Prediction Models Based on Deep Learning
authors: Ao, X.; Gong, Y.; He, A.
tldr: Comprehensive survey of deep learning time series prediction models covering CNN, RNN, Transformer, GNN, and hybrid architectures with a task-oriented model selection framework.
problem_and_motivation: Existing surveys of deep learning for time series prediction lack practical model selection guidelines, sufficient cross-model comparative analysis, and adequate coverage of strategies for emerging challenges like interpretability and computational efficiency. Researchers face significant challenges in selecting appropriate models based on intrinsic properties, data characteristics, and task requirements.
approach: Systematically reviews CNN-based models including TCN, SCINet, and Kmeans-CNN with comparative analysis.
Analyzes RNN-based models including LSTM and GRU, focusing on gating mechanisms for long-term dependency capture.
Examines Transformer variants including Informer, Autoformer, iTransformer, Scaleformer, and CrossFormer.
Reviews GNN-based methods including STGCN, MTGNN, DSTAGNN, and HGCN-MA for multivariate spatiotemporal forecasting.
Evaluates hybrid models combining deep learning with statistical methods such as ARIMA-RNN, ETSformer, N-BEATS, and PatchTST.
Proposes a task-driven model selection framework mapping problem characteristics to optimal model classes.
Conducts cross-model and cross-dataset meta-analysis identifying broader architectural trends and trade-offs.
findings: Transformer variants dominate long-term dependency capture in multivariate settings with sequences exceeding 1000 steps.
num: Informer reduces attention complexity from O(L squared) to O(L log L) via ProbSparse mechanism.
num: ETSformer reduces inference latency by 37% vs. Autoformer on ETT data while maintaining accuracy.
num: PatchTST achieves 23% lower MSE than Informer with 60% less GPU memory.
GNN-based models significantly outperform channel-independent models when strong spatial or relational dependencies exist.
iTransformer achieves state-of-the-art results on multivariate benchmarks without predefined graphs.
GRUs remain competitive for medium-length sequences around 100-1000 steps with low-latency inference requirements.
Hybrid models frequently top benchmark leaderboards due to ability to separate and model different temporal components.
Decomposition is a recurring key design pattern among the most generalizable Transformer variants.
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: Structure of one-dimensional CNN -> CNNs extract local spatial patterns via convolutional filters and pooling.
Figure 2: Structure of dilated causal convolution -> Dilated convolution expands receptive field exponentially.
Figure 3: Structure of TCN residual block -> Residual connections alleviate vanishing gradients in deep networks.
Figure 4: Structure of simple RNN -> RNNs maintain hidden state as memory of past sequential inputs.
Figure 5: Structure of LSTM -> LSTM uses three gates to control information flow for long-term dependency capture.
Figure 6: Structure of GRU -> GRU merges forget and input gates into update gate reducing complexity.
Figure 7: Structure of Transformer -> Self-attention mechanism enables parallel sequence modeling without recurrence.
Figure 8: Structure of Informer -> ProbSparse attention and distilling layers enable efficient long-sequence processing.
Figure 9: Structure of Autoformer -> Auto-correlation mechanism and series decomposition replace standard attention.
Figure 10: Structure of iTransformer -> Inverted architecture treats variables as tokens for multivariate modeling.
Figure 11: Structure of GNN -> GNNs model spatial dependencies via graph convolution and temporal dependencies via temporal convolution.
Figure 12: Task-driven model selection framework -> Maps problem characteristics to optimal model classes.
Table 1: Analysis of CNN-based algorithms -> CNN for short-term, TCN for long-sequence, SCINet for seasonal data.
Table 2: Analysis of RNN-based algorithms -> RNN foundational, LSTM for long-sequence, GRU for resource-constrained scenarios.
Table 3: Analysis of Transformer-based algorithms -> Various Transformer variants optimized for different forecasting scenarios.

definitions.definition: Convolutional Neural Network, extracts local spatial features via sliding kernels.
Temporal Convolutional Network, uses dilated causal convolutions for long-range temporal dependencies.
Recurrent Neural Network, processes sequential data by maintaining hidden state memory.
Long Short-Term Memory network, uses gating mechanisms to capture long-term dependencies.
Gated Recurrent Unit, simplified LSTM variant with update and reset gates.
Architecture relying on self-attention mechanism for parallel sequence modeling.
Efficient Transformer variant using ProbSparse attention for long-sequence time series forecasting.
Transformer variant using auto-correlation mechanism and series decomposition for forecasting.
Inverted Transformer that treats variables as tokens for multivariate time series modeling.
Graph Neural Network, models relational dependencies via graph structures.
Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network for fixed-topology spatiotemporal data.
Multivariate Time Series Graph Neural Network with end-to-end dynamic graph learning.
Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for interpretable time series forecasting via decomposition.
Patch-based Transformer splitting series into overlapping sub-series tokens for efficient long-horizon modeling.
SHapley Additive exPlanations, game-theoretic approach for feature importance attribution.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, approximates model locally with interpretable surrogate.
AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average, traditional statistical model for linear time series forecasting.
Exponential Smoothing State Space model for time series with trend and seasonality components.
Fast Fourier Transform for extracting frequency-domain correlation features from time series.

topics.name: Forecasting Algorithms for Sequential Spending Data

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a comprehensive review and systematic comparison of five major deep learning model families for time series prediction: CNNs, RNNs, Transformers, GNNs, and hybrid models. It establishes a task-oriented framework that maps problem characteristics such as sequence length, multivariate dependencies, and computational constraints to optimal model classes.
directly_justifies: LSTM and GRU are foundational architectures for capturing long-term dependencies in sequential financial data.
Transformer variants dominate multivariate time series forecasting with sequences exceeding 1000 steps.
iTransformer treats variables as tokens achieving state-of-the-art results on multivariate benchmarks.
Hybrid models combining statistical and deep learning methods frequently top benchmark leaderboards.
Task-driven model selection framework maps problem characteristics to optimal model classes.
limits: The review focuses on general time series benchmarks rather than personal finance or spending-specific datasets.
Evaluation is based on reported results across heterogeneous benchmarks rather than standardized comparative experiments.
The paper does not address anomaly detection or unsupervised spending pattern analysis specifically.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. The paper is a general survey of deep learning models for time series prediction and does not address personal finance systems, Filipino demographics, budgeting strategies, or mobile-first design. It was flagged as relevant to domains 6.A and 6.B at medium relevance because the reviewed predictive models are directly applicable to financial time series forecasting tasks including spending prediction. All other domains were considered and rejected.

limitations: Survey synthesizes existing literature rather than presenting new experimental results.
Evaluation is based on reported results from heterogeneous benchmarks, limiting direct comparability.
Does not address personal finance application contexts or domain-specific constraints.
The review does not cover recent foundation models or large language models adapted for time series.
remember_this: Transformer variants with decomposition mechanisms achieve best generalization across time series domains.
Informer reduces attention complexity from O(L squared) to O(L log L) enabling long-sequence processing.
PatchTST achieves 23% lower MSE than Informer with 60% less GPU memory via patch tokenization.
Hybrid models combining statistical and deep learning methods consistently outperform pure approaches.
No universally optimal model exists; selection must match model strengths to task requirements and constraints.
